newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Sanford blames NZD, markets for H1 loss.
newsitem.headline: Sanford blames NZD, markets for H1 loss.

text.p: Fishing company Sanford Ltd said on Tuesday a significant reduction in forward cover, a stronger New Zealand dollar and weaker markets had taken it into a loss for the first half to February 28.
The company added the second six months would continue to be difficult, but that a similar trading contribution as the first half was achievable as long as the currency did not strengthen further.
Sanford made a loss of NZ$1.46 million in the first half against an $11.67 million profit a year earlier.
Sanford said the yen had weakened by 21 percent against the New Zealand dollar over the last 12 months.
There had been generally weaker markets for fin fish and aquaculture production.
Cost recovery charges imposed by the government had been set at artificially high levels.
Sanford also lashed out at the Reserve Bank's zero to three percent annual inflation target.
"Government should be aware that the stability of the export sector for primary production is now seriously affected as a result of pre-occupation with inflation," it said.
Furthermore, strength in the New Zealand dollar had not meant cheaper import costs.
Sanford's Iquique plant in northern Chile had been closed and losses curtailed. Its San Antonio plant had only operated spasmodically and losses were continuing.

"In view of the uncertainty in relation to the current and future viability of the San Antonio plant and questions over the resource itself, directors have decided to write off the total residual capital value of the investment in Chile of NZ$8.870m which represents 3.5 percent of shareholders equity," Sanford said.
The action would allow the company to concentrate on improving the profitability of the mainstream business operations in New Zealand and overseas.
Sanford revealed that it had taken a 40 percent equity interest in a Namibian company, with the balance being controlled by indigenous interests.
The company had been granted term quota and exploratory fishing concessions in Namibian waters for orange roughy, alfonsino and other deep water species.
The company's entry into Namibia is by way of the transfer of vessels, not cash.
